outcome.answer:
Dense-to-sparse retrieval is covered in several ways here. Some papers explicitly convert dense retrievers into sparse ones: Latent Terms shows dense retrievers can be decomposed into BM25-ready sparse features with sparse autoencoders, without sparse supervision or expansion training, and can match or beat the base single-vector scorer [2]. SPLARE likewise uses sparse autoencoders as the basis for learned sparse retrieval, aiming for more structured and expressive sparse features than vocabulary-based methods, with strong multilingual and out-of-domain results [7].

Other papers focus on sparse alternatives that reach dense-like effectiveness or replace dense/multi-vector indexing with sparse coding. LACONIC is a learned sparse retriever designed to bridge the gap to dense models while using much less index memory [1]. SSR replaces multi-vector dense retrieval and clustering with sparse coding and inverted indexing, improving indexing time, latency, and retrieval quality [10]. Sparse Coverage maps local dense span embeddings to sparse centers for patent retrieval [5]. If you mean combining dense and sparse rather than converting between them, one paper studies tuned dense-sparse fusion for hybrid retrieval [9].
